tiers.everyday: Famous eruptions and earthquakes on the globe, from Vesuvius in 79 CE to Mount St. Helens in 1980. Most pins are official published points from NOAA; the Vesuvius 79 link uses Pompeii's Pleiades point. Every number names its source.
tiers.student: A curated first batch from the NOAA NCEI Significant Volcanic Eruptions and Significant Earthquake databases (doi:10.7289/V5JW8BSH, doi:10.7289/V5TD9V7K), with USGS pages for context. Where NCEI and USGS give different death tolls, both are shown. Pins are NCEI's published points, so they are approximate, except the Vesuvius 79 link, which uses Pompeii's Pleiades point.

facts.text: NCEI rates the 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius VEI 5 and counts 2,100 deaths, dated 25 August 79.
The USGS deadliest-eruptions table gives 3,360, mainly from pyroclastic flow.
The 79 CE eruption buried Herculaneum and Pompeii and was described in letters by Pliny the Younger.
USGS counts eight major explosive eruptions since a caldera formed about 17,000 years ago.
Eruptions were frequent from 1631 to 1944; the most recent eruption was in 1944.
The INGV Vesuvius Observatory, founded in 1841, is the first volcano observatory in the world.
NCEI links this eruption to an earthquake record and a tsunami record.
NOAA NCEI Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database, event 1348
Other published dates for the eruption: not reviewed [UNKNOWN]; only the NCEI date is shown

steps.text: On 1 November 1755 a great earthquake struck under the Atlantic off Portugal. NCEI lists magnitude 8.5 and 50,000 deaths.
A tsunami followed. On the shores of Portugal and Morocco it climbed roughly 5 to 15 m, and the Azores and Madeira also saw large waves.
The waves crossed the ocean: far-away accounts come from Caribbean islands, Brazil and Newfoundland.
Scientists still disagree about which fault broke. One study modelled a source south of Gorringe Bank; a later one found the Marquês de Pombal fault fitted best.
Next: the Atlas entry on earthquakes and plate faults, for how faults break.

stories.title: Tambora 1815 and Krakatau 1883: eruptions felt worldwide

steps.text: April 1815: Tambora erupts. NCEI rates it VEI 7, the highest in this batch.
The death toll is disputed: NCEI counts 60,000 in total, USGS 92,000, mostly from starvation.
August 1883: Krakatau explodes. The sound was heard about 5,000 km away.
The tsunami killed most of the roughly 36,000 victims.
Both eruptions put sulfate aerosols high into the atmosphere, and USGS says that cools the climate. Krakatau's dust lowered global temperatures and caused vivid sunsets.
Compare a modern eruption: Mount St. Helens in 1980 was VEI 5, with 57 deaths.
